key_facts: Self-limiting rash of young people: a **herald patch** then oval pink patches with a **collarette of scale** in a 'Christmas tree' pattern on the trunk.
Incidence about **0.5–2%**; most common at **10–35 years**, often in spring and autumn.
Probably triggered by reactivation of **HHV-6/7**; not contagious in practice.
Reassure; emollient and a mild or moderate topical steroid or antihistamine for itch. Resolves in **6–12 weeks**.
In **pregnancy** (first 15 weeks) there are reports of miscarriage: inform the obstetric team. Consider secondary syphilis if palms or soles are involved.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Diagnosis confirmed from the course case:** the case shows a single initial lesion (Picture 1) followed ~2 weeks later by a generalised eruption (Picture 2) after a URTI. The diagnosis is **pityriasis rosea**; guttate psoriasis was listed as a **differential**, not the answer. The key mimic to exclude is **secondary syphilis** as the must-not-miss differential.

A common, **self-limiting** papulosquamous eruption of adolescents and young adults (10–35 years), beginning with a single **herald patch** followed days to ~2 weeks later by a **secondary eruption** of smaller oval scaly patches on the trunk and proximal limbs. Lasts about **6–12 weeks** (most 6–8). Recurrence is uncommon (~2–3%).

sub: Teenagers and young adults (10–35 years); slightly more common in women.
Incidence about 0.5–2%; seasonal clustering in spring and autumn.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Cause not proven; strongest evidence links it to **reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and 7 (HHV-6/HHV-7)** — supported by preceding URTI/prodrome, seasonal clustering, and low recurrence. **PR-like (pityriasiform) drug eruptions** occur with e.g. ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, isotretinoin, gold, some biologics/vaccines — these lack a herald patch and persist while the drug continues.

ul: **HHV-6 and HHV-7** reactivation is the strongest association.
**Drug-induced** PR-like eruptions: ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, metronidazole, isotretinoin, imatinib and others.
Reported after vaccines (BCG, influenza, COVID-19) and viral infections.
**"It's ringworm"**: tinea has an advancing scaly edge; PR has trailing scale just inside the edge.
**"It's catching"**: it is not considered contagious.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: PR is thought to be a **T-cell response to reactivated HHV-6/7**, following skin tension lines.

mech.t: HHV-6/7 reactivate (often after a mild viral illness), triggering a cell-mediated immune response in the skin.
A single 2–5 cm oval pink patch appears first, often on the trunk.
1–2 weeks later many smaller ovals appear along **cleavage (Langer) lines**, giving the Christmas-tree pattern.
mech.caption: Oval patches following the ribs: the Christmas-tree pattern on the back.

mech.t: Scale sits **just inside the edge**, trailing behind it, unlike tinea where scale is at the advancing edge.
mech.caption: Pityriasis rosea collarette (trailing scale) vs tinea (scale at the advancing edge).

histo: Mild spongiosis with focal parakeratosis (mounds), extravasated red cells and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.
Biopsy only if atypical or persistent beyond 3 months.

ul: Possible prodrome: malaise, headache, sore throat, low-grade fever (URTI — Case 3).
**Herald patch:** single, 2–5 cm, oval, salmon-pink (grey-brown/violaceous in darker skin) plaque with fine **collarette scale** inside the edge; often trunk, upper arm, neck, thigh.

**Secondary eruption** (after ~1–2 weeks): many smaller oval macules/plaques with collarette scale, long axes along skin cleavage lines → **"Christmas-tree" pattern** on the back, "V" on the chest; usually spares face, scalp, palms and soles.
Itch: none to moderate (~25% significant).
Variants: **inverse** (flexural — axillae/groin, commoner in children/skin of colour), papular, vesicular, purpuric, urticarial, giant, unilateral, oral lesions.
Darker skin: more papular/facial lesions; prolonged post-inflammatory hyper/hypopigmentation.

variants.name: Secondary syphilis
variants.t: Copper-red palm / sole papules. *Site: Palms, soles.*

sub: Lesions look grey-brown or violaceous; papular and inverse (flexural) forms are more common; pigment change can persist.
Possible link with miscarriage in the first 15 weeks: inform the obstetric team.

ul: **Syphilis serology** (treponemal EIA ± RPR) if atypical, palms/soles involved, no herald patch, sexual risk, or lasting >12 weeks.
**Skin scrapings for mycology** if the herald patch alone looks like tinea (scale at advancing edge).
Drug history (pityriasiform drug eruption).
Biopsy rarely (atypical/persistent).
Pregnancy test/status relevant — see 3.6.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses

ddx.name: Guttate psoriasis
ddx.f: Many small drop papules, thicker silvery scale, **no herald patch**, after strep throat.

ddx.name: Secondary syphilis
ddx.f: Palms / soles, mucous patches, nodes, malaise; positive serology.

ddx.name: Tinea corporis
ddx.f: Active scaly edge, central clearing; KOH +.

ddx.name: Pityriasiform drug eruption
ddx.f: New drug, no herald patch, persists.

blocks: **Guttate psoriasis** is an acute eruption of small (<1 cm) drop-like scaly papules/plaques, typically in children, teens, and young adults — often **1–3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis**. Module 4 Spot Diagnosis consensus: widespread scaly eruption on trunk/limbs in a 14-year-old with no prior skin disease → **guttate psoriasis**. Main clinical DDx: **pityriasis rosea**.

ul: Same psoriatic immune axis; strong link to **Group A streptococcus** and HLA-C*06:02-enriched early-onset disease.
May be first presentation of psoriasis or remain a one-off self-limited episode.
PR (DDx): putative viral trigger; herald patch then secondary oval plaques on Langer lines.
Clinical. Ask about sore throat; consider throat swab / ASO if indicated.
Look for herald patch and Christmas-tree pattern to favour PR.
Biopsy rarely needed.
Consider syphilis serology if PR-like but atypical (palms/soles, systemic, persistent).
Emollients; mild–potent TCS matched to extent/site; vitamin D analogues sometimes.
Treat proven strep infection per local antimicrobial guidance (treating strep does not always clear guttate quickly).
Counsel possible recurrence or later plaque psoriasis.
Reassure; emollient ± mild TCS for itch; UV advice individualised; refer if severe/atypical.
Teen + abrupt drop-like scaly rash + recent sore throat ≈ guttate until proven otherwise.
Avoid oral steroids.
Safety-net return if eruption becomes confluent, pustular, or erythrodermic.

sections.title: Management
blocks: Based on NICE CKS *Pityriasis rosea* and PCDS/BAD leaflet themes:

ul: Explain benign, **non-contagious**, self-limiting (6–12 weeks); no isolation needed; scars do not occur (pigment change may persist months in darker skin).
Emollients and soap substitutes; avoid hot showers, perfumed products, tight clothes; moderate sun exposure may speed resolution in some.

Itch: emollient ± **mild–moderate topical corticosteroid** (e.g. clobetasone butyrate 0.05%) short course to itchy areas; **sedating antihistamine** at night (e.g. chlorphenamine; counsel drowsiness) or non-sedating by day.
Evidence for **high-dose aciclovir** early in extensive/symptomatic disease is limited — specialist decision.

blocks.h: Guttate psoriasis (if that is the diagnosis instead)

ul: Throat swab only if sore throat ongoing (treat streptococcal infection per NG84); emollients; topical vitamin D analogue ± topical steroid, coal-tar; refer dermatology for **NB-UVB phototherapy** if widespread/distressing (lesions too numerous for topicals). Often clears in 3–4 months; ~⅓ later develop chronic plaque psoriasis.

ladder.t: Benign, **non-contagious**, settles in 6–12 weeks; no isolation; no scarring (pigment may linger).
Emollients, soap substitutes; avoid hot showers, perfumes, tight clothes; moderate sun may help.
**Mild–moderate topical steroid** (e.g. clobetasone butyrate 0.05%) short course; sedating antihistamine at night or non-sedating by day.
High-dose aciclovir early in extensive disease: limited evidence, specialist decision.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Oral steroids**: Don’t: may prolong or worsen PR.

refer.t: Palm / sole lesions, mouth ulcers, nodes or sexual risk: **syphilis serology** and sexual health.
PR in the **first 15 weeks of pregnancy**: inform midwife / obstetric team.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Palm or sole lesions, mouth ulcers, lymphadenopathy or sexual risk: **syphilis serology** and sexual-health referral.
Pityriasis rosea in the **first 15 weeks of pregnancy**: inform the midwife or obstetric team.
Lasting more than 3 months: reconsider the diagnosis.
**Pregnancy:** PR in pregnancy (esp. first 15 weeks) has been associated with miscarriage/premature delivery — inform/refer to midwife/obstetrician (CKS).
Atypical features, palms/soles/mucosal involvement or sexual risk → **syphilis serology / refer to sexual health (GUM)**.
Persisting >12 weeks, diagnostic doubt, severe symptoms → GP/dermatology.
Suspected drug cause → review medication with prescriber.
Itch; post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation lasting months.
Pregnancy complications (rare reports).
Resolves spontaneously in 6–12 weeks; recurrence is uncommon.

pearls: "One big patch first, then many small ovals along the ribs" = PR; "shower of small drops after strep throat" = guttate psoriasis.
The herald patch is often mis-treated as ringworm — antifungal failure is a clue.
**Every generalised papulosquamous rash: ask about sexual history and look at palms and soles.**
Do not prescribe oral steroids for PR (may prolong/worsen).
Provide BAD/PCDS patient leaflet; review if not resolving by 3 months.

quiz.q: Where is the scale on a herald patch?
quiz.a: A collarette just inside the edge (tinea: at the advancing edge).
Atypical, palms / soles, no herald patch, sexual risk, or > 12 weeks.
Inform the midwife / obstetric team (miscarriage risk).
